definition: Shockingly bad in a way that is obvious to anyone who notices it.
example: The bank's egregious billing mistake charged the family for the same purchase forty times.
nuance: Egregious stresses how glaring and extreme a wrong is; flagrant adds that it was done openly, often on purpose.
prompt: A health inspector walks through a restaurant kitchen during a surprise visit.
options: Keeping raw chicken above the salad greens was an egregious lapse.
The egregious cook chatted warmly with every guest who came in.
The inspector praised the kitchen's egregious cleanliness and gave it top marks.
She found one tiny, egregious crumb that posed no risk at all.
reasons: An obvious, serious food-safety failure is exactly the kind of wrong the word describes.
This confuses the word with gregarious, which means sociable and friendly.
The word condemns something as terrible, so it cannot describe praiseworthy cleanliness.
A harmless, barely noticeable crumb is neither glaring nor seriously bad.

practice.prompt: A student proofreads a classmate's history report before it is turned in.
options: Being egregious, Marco eagerly joined every group discussion in class.
The report had one egregious typo so subtle that nobody noticed it.
Dating the first moon landing to 1869 was an egregious error.
Her egregious research was so thorough that the teacher gave it top marks.
reasons: Enjoying group conversation describes being gregarious, a look-alike word.
An egregious flaw stands out; one that nobody notices cannot be glaring.
Missing the date by a whole century is a glaring, serious mistake anyone would catch.
Thorough, excellent work is the opposite of something shockingly bad.
